job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817: Loopholes, Ambiguities, and Drafting Problems
*(Manager's amendment text of Oct. 6, 2026)*

## Sec. 2: Definitions

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-ton cap applies "by a single vessel," so an operator could spread recovery across several vessels, each under the limit, with no aggregation rule by operator, project, or license area.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "per year."** The bill doesn't say whether this means a calendar year, a rolling 12 months, or a license year. That uncertainty makes it hard to know when a violation begins.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), wet vs. dry tonnage.** "Metric tons" isn't specified as wet or dry weight. Nodules hold substantial water when lifted, so the choice can move an operation above or below the threshold.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "recovery" and "by a vessel."** Modern systems use a seabed collector, a riser, and a surface ship. It's unclear whether recovery happens at collection or at lift, and whether collector vehicles or stationary platforms count as "vessels" at all.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "other mineral resources" and the 200-meter line.** "Mineral resources" is undefined, and the bill doesn't say how depth is measured (below sea surface or mean low water). The definition may also sweep in unrelated activity like deep sand, gravel, or phosphate dredging, which invites overbreadth challenges.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "seabed."** Subsea-floor extraction (e.g., drilling or tunneling into subsoil) arguably isn't recovery "from the seabed."

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B), undefined "Secretary."** No Secretary is identified (Commerce? Interior?), so the open-ended catch-all has no clear administering official.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(B), vagueness and delegation.** "Risks... comparable to" is standardless, and the provision sets no procedure (notice-and-comment, findings, review). Because it can make conduct criminal under Sec. 5(b), it's exposed to void-for-vagueness, nondelegation, and fair-notice challenges.

9. **Sec. 2(2), entity types.** "Corporation" omits LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other entities, which are common structures for mining ventures.

10. **Sec. 2(2), jurisdiction of organization.** Only entities organized under "the laws of a State" are covered. Without a definition of "State," entities organized in DC or the territories, or under federal charter, may fall outside.

11. **Sec. 2(2), no ownership or control test.** Foreign-incorporated subsidiaries owned or controlled by U.S. companies are not U.S. persons. Lawful permanent residents are also excluded.

12. **Sec. 2(3), "covered vessel" disconnected from the prohibition.** The term is used only in the Sec. 4 registry, not in Sec. 3. Vessels under 5,000 gross tons escape registration entirely, and "equipped for the recovery" is undefined.

## Sec. 3: Prohibition

13. **Sec. 3(a), "in the United States."** The bill doesn't say whether this covers the territorial sea, the EEZ, or the outer continental shelf. Combined with item 11, a foreign entity operating on the high seas is plainly outside the bill even if U.S. capital and management stand behind it.

14. **Sec. 3(a), narrow scope of conduct.** Only "engag[ing] in" mining is barred. Nothing prohibits financing, chartering, aiding, importing, or processing nodules recovered abroad, so U.S. firms could support offshore operations and buy their output.

15. **Sec. 3(a), "person" undefined.** It's unclear whether federal, state, or foreign-government entities are covered.

16. **Sec. 3(b), unbounded grandfather clause.** The clause exempts mining under "an exploration license" without limiting it to licenses issued by the U.S. or under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (DSHMRA). It may therefore cover foreign-state or ISA-sponsored contracts as well.

17. **Sec. 3(b), no limits on duration, renewal, transfer, or area.** The exemption has no time limit, doesn't address renewals, extensions, amendments, or assignments, and isn't confined to the licensed area or the activities the license authorized.

18. **Sec. 3(b), internal contradiction.** The clause exempts "mining" under an exploration license, which by definition doesn't authorize commercial recovery. Courts could read it either as a narrow exemption for exploration or as a broad safe harbor for commercial-scale recovery by license holders.

19. **Sec. 3(b), incentive to rush.** Because the cutoff is enactment, applicants have every reason to secure licenses before the bill is signed.

20. **Sec. 3(c), self-declared purpose test.** The environmental-assessment exemption has no definition, tonnage cap, approval requirement, duration, or oversight. Any operation, including commercial-scale "test mining," could claim the purpose.

## Sec. 4: Registry

21. **Sec. 4, no penalty.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register or report, or filing a false report, carries no penalty under this Act. Criminal false-statement liability under 18 U.S.C. § 1001 may still apply.

22. **Sec. 4, no content, deadline, or verification.** Reports are self-certified and need not include tonnage, location, or depth. There is no registration deadline, no inspection, observer, or vessel-tracking authority, no rulemaking grant to NOAA, and "operator" is undefined.

23. **Sec. 4, jurisdictional reach.** The section doesn't say whether foreign-flagged vessels or vessels operating outside U.S. waters must register.

## Sec. 5: Penalties

24. **Sec. 5(a), conflict with the effective date.** Civil penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but Sec. 8 makes the Act effective 180 days later. That inconsistency is an easy basis for contesting penalties in the interim window.

25. **Sec. 5(a), day-counting vs. annual threshold.** The violation is defined by annual tonnage, but the penalty runs "for each day." It's unclear which days are violation days: all days of operation, or only days after the threshold is crossed.

26. **Sec. 5(a), no enforcement machinery.** The bill names no enforcing agency and provides no administrative process, hearing, judicial review, venue, statute of limitations, injunctive relief, or forfeiture authority.

27. **Sec. 5(a), Excessive Fines argument.** An uncapped $1,000,000-per-day penalty, with no gradation by severity, invites an Eighth Amendment challenge, especially for marginal threshold exceedances.

28. **Sec. 5(b), willfulness tied to vague standards.** Criminal liability for "willful" violations of a prohibition whose scope partly depends on unspecified Secretary determinations (item 8) strengthens fair-notice and rule-of-lenity defenses.

## Sec. 6: International Agreement

29. **Sec. 6, hortatory and ambiguous deadline.** "Shall seek to negotiate" imposes no enforceable obligation. "Not later than 18 months" could mean the deadline to begin or to conclude negotiations, and there is no reporting requirement or consequence for failure.

## Sec. 7: Duration

30. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b), direct conflict.** Subsection (a) keeps the prohibition in effect until Congress acts by joint resolution, while (b) ends the whole Act at 10 years. Which controls is unclear.

31. **Sec. 7(a), no study mandate.** The National Academies report is a precondition, but nothing directs or funds the study. "Serious harm" is undefined, and a joint resolution is in practice no different from ordinary repeal legislation.

32. **Sec. 7(b), no savings clause.** When the Act expires, pending civil and criminal enforcement actions may be extinguished. Whether the general savings statute (1 U.S.C. § 109) applies to an expiration, as opposed to a repeal, is contestable.

33. **Sec. 7(b) and Sec. 8, effective span.** The sunset is measured from enactment, but the Act takes effect 180 days later, so the prohibition actually runs about 9.5 years.

## Sec. 8 and Structural Gaps

34. **Sec. 8, 180-day window.** Operators can conduct unrestricted recovery between enactment and the effective date, subject to the conflict noted in item 24.

35. **No coordination with DSHMRA.** The bill doesn't amend or repeal the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. § 1401 et seq.). That leaves NOAA's existing exploration-license and commercial-recovery-permit authority intact, and implied repeal is disfavored, so the two statutes would conflict.

36. **No severability clause.** If a court strikes Sec. 2(1)(B) or the penalty provisions, there's no express direction on whether the remainder survives.

37. **No rulemaking authority.** No agency is given authority to issue implementing regulations, define terms, or fill the gaps above, which leaves interpretation to litigation.

## Most Consequential for Markup

The highest-impact items are:
- the multi-vessel and corporate-structure gaps (1, 9–11, 13–14),
- the open-ended Sec. 3(b) and 3(c) exemptions (16–20),
- the Sec. 7 conflict (30),
- the DSHMRA gap (35), and
- the constitutional exposure of Sec. 2(1)(B) and Sec. 5 (8, 27, 28).

Expect sponsors to try to fix some of these, especially items 24 and 30, which read like clerical errors, so they may close before or during markup. I'd recommend outside counsel review the constitutional and DSHMRA arguments before anyone relies on them publicly.
